questions.q: What three themes organize Young's principles for mastery?
a: Seeing, doing and feedback
Reading, writing and arithmetic
Planning, practice and rest
Focus, speed and memory
questions.why: The overview groups the maxims into learning from others, practicing well, and adjusting in the real world.

questions.q: How does the summary describe a problem space?
a: A maze where you know your position and the destination
A ladder of increasingly difficult tasks
A map that has no fixed endpoint
A puzzle with only one possible solution
questions.why: The first lesson says the walls limit your moves and you must search for the path that reaches the exit.

questions.q: What image did Andrew Wiles use for working on a hard proof?
a: Stumbling around a dark mansion until you find the light switch
Climbing a mountain one camp at a time
Solving a crossword with a team of friends
Following a map someone else drew for you
questions.why: The first lesson uses Wiles, who solved Fermat's Last Theorem, to show how solutions accumulate slowly.

questions.q: Why does Young prefer variation over repetition in practice?
a: It helps skills transfer to new situations
It makes every practice session shorter
It removes the need for feedback
It builds muscle memory much faster
questions.why: The second lesson draws on 1940s jazz musicians who learned by playing with many different people.

questions.q: What does renovating instead of rebuilding mean?
a: Replacing old ideas and habits one at a time
Abandoning everything you know and starting over
Redecorating your workspace to focus better
Repeating the basics until they feel new
questions.why: The third lesson's unlearning strategy keeps what works and swaps out single pieces until a new approach fits.
